The reported coefficient of thermal expansion of Alnekar glass-ceramic is 3.1 µm/m·K (with an uncertainty of ±0.05 µm/m·K according to the primary measurement). This figure is very firmly grounded in reliable evidence. It appears consistently across five independent sources: (1) an original dilatometry report from University of Northton's Materials Characterisation Facility using standard push-rod dilatometer methodology with documented measurement uncertainty; (2) the manufacturer's certified property sheet filed under industrial materials certification requirements with third-party inspection; (3) the original patent disclosure by the material's inventor, citing ASTM E228-compliant testing; (4) a materials handbook citing the university study; and (5) an engineering reference work citing the patent. The convergence of this value across manufacturer certification, independent university testing, patent disclosure, and secondary references—all using standard dilatometric methods over the same temperature range (25–300 °C)—indicates the figure is well-established and reliable for practical engineering applications.

According to the sources, Enyali Zofren is said to have been born in Thalorune (specifically in the south riverside quarter) on 3rd Bloomrise 1283. The evidence is very solid and comes from multiple independent contemporary sources: (1) the official City of Thalorune Birth Register (P1), an original primary document signed and sealed by the Thalorune Civic Archive; (2) the Thalorune Meridian Observatory's night-book (P2), an original astronomical record commissioned by the Guild of Midwives; and (3) a personal letter (P3) from a witness (Alira Senn, apparently a midwife) dated just two days after the birth, describing the delivery in Thalorune. These three independent original sources all corroborate the birthplace consistently. Secondary sources (P4, P5) cite and confirm these primary documents. The convergence of official civic registration, astronomical records, and eyewitness testimony provides exceptionally strong evidence for this birthplace.

Modern write-ups attribute the idiom 'clacking the jore' to Lonnic Forge. The evidence for this attribution appears moderately secure but not unassailable. The primary foundation is a 1794 payroll ledger from Lonnic Forge (P1) in which the head clerk explicitly states the phrase 'is said to have originated' there—notably using reported speech rather than claiming direct knowledge. This is corroborated by an 1852 legal deposition (P3) that independently references the same origin. However, the chain of attestation then becomes circular: a 2021 academic journal article (P4) cites only the 1794 ledger, and an encyclopedia entry (P5) cites a 1907 dialect recording (P2) where an elderly retired smith reports what 'they'll tell you'—again, secondhand attribution rather than primary knowledge. The 1794 ledger remains the earliest written source, but its phrasing ('is said to have originated') suggests the origin claim was already folkloric even then, not necessarily factual. The later sources largely reinforce each other without introducing independent evidence of actual genesis at that location. While Lonnic Forge has strong documentary backing as the *stated* birthplace, the evidence does not definitively prove the idiom actually originated there, only that this origin story was firmly established and repeatedly affirmed.

According to the available pages, the unemployment rate claimed for Myrava Province in 2011 is 18.4%. This number appears to be very firmly established, as it is consistently reported across multiple independent and official sources: (1) the Provincial Gazette of Myrava (P1) — the official government statistical publication compiled under the Statistics Ordinance; (2) the Labour Force Household Survey 2011 (P2) — a large-scale survey with 18,207 respondents and a 95% confidence interval of ±0.6%; (3) a ministerial statement to the Legislative Assembly (P3) citing official Directorate figures; and (4) academic and reference sources (P4, P5) that cite the primary official sources. The consistency across these independent sources — official statistics, survey data, government statements, and academic literature — all converging on the identical figure of 18.4% provides strong corroboration.

Keira Lomhost is credited with being the first to complete the solitary circumnavigation of the Murrillon Sea in March 2003. This claim is very well established, supported by multiple independent and complementary sources: (1) the official Murrillon Sailing Federation registry (P1) with GPS tracking, harbor-master inspection, and sworn statement; (2) contemporaneous lighthouse keeper's logbook notation (P3) from her return date; (3) satellite position data from MMOC showing continuous 15-minute-interval tracking over the complete route (P2); and (4) independent scholarly and encyclopedic sources (P4, P5) that cite the primary evidence. The convergence of real-time satellite verification, official certification, independent eyewitness account, and subsequent documentation across multiple authoritative sources makes this one of the most robustly established claims in the retrieved results.

Lake Namaruk is attributed a depth of 1,024 m (maximum recorded depth). This figure is very well documented. It appears consistently across multiple independent sources using different methodologies: (1) the official 2019 government register based on commissioned depth soundings, (2) a 2022 bathymetric survey using multibeam sonar by the R/V Pelikan with precise coordinates, and (3) a 2021 university core drilling that reached lakebed at the same depth. All three primary sources independently report 1,024 m, and secondary sources cite these findings. The convergence of evidence from official government measurement, professional hydrographic surveying, and academic core drilling provides strong documentation of this figure.

The commonly cited figure for the average lifespan of a wild Zephrite cloud-otter is 27 years. This figure is quite solidly supported by multiple independent, methodologically rigorous primary sources: (1) the National Faunal Statistics Office compiled data from 3,418 carcass reports with verified ages of death (2010-2022); (2) the Albary Museum analyzed 61 wild-collected specimens using tooth-cementum analysis with recorded birth and death dates; and (3) the Gullstream Biological Station conducted a prospective telemetry study tracking 142 wild individuals to natural death, yielding a mean of 27 years (SD = 3.1). All three independent datasets converge on the same figure, each based on direct observation and specimens from different time periods and geographic/methodological contexts. Secondary sources (P4, P5) that cite these primary sources further reinforce the consistency of this estimate. The evidence is particularly strong because of the convergence across different data-collection methods (mortality records, museum specimens, and live tracking) and the substantial sample sizes involved.

According to common online sources, the Silaron woodcurl plane was invented in 1894. The evidence for this date is very solid, supported by multiple independent and convergent sources: (1) a patent filing dated 17 March 1894 with grant date of 8 September 1894 (P1), (2) contemporaneous workshop diary entries from the inventor Jorin F. Silaron dated 12-13 April 1894 (P3), (3) metallurgical and chronological analysis of the prototype (Pb-210/Bi-210 isotopic dating and die-strike font matching) both confirming 1894 ± 2 years (P2), and (4) a peer-reviewed feature article in Tool History Quarterly citing the patent record (P4). The convergence of primary sources (patent, diary, artifact analysis) and secondary scholarship creates strong corroboration for the 1894 invention date.
